en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Saṅghādisesa-kanda
10. The Training Rule on Renouncing the Training At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, having quarreled with the bhikkhunīs, being angry and displeased, spoke thus:
“I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training.

What indeed are these female ascetics, these daughters of the Sakyans? There are other female ascetics who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... [as before]... they complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How indeed can the noble lady Caṇḍakāḷī, being angry and displeased, speak thus:
‘I renounce the Buddha … I renounce the training.

What use are these ascetic women who are daughters of the Sakyans? There are other ascetic women who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life’? …pe…
“Is it true, monks, that the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, being angry and displeased, spoke thus:
‘I renounce the Buddha … I renounce the training.

What have these ascetics to do with me, these ascetics who are daughters of the Sakyans? There are other ascetics who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life’?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can this be, monks? How can the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, being angry and displeased, speak thus?”
‘I renounce the Buddha … [and so on] … I renounce the training.
What indeed are these nuns who are daughters of the Sakyans? There are other nuns who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [and so on].”
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whichever nun, being angry and displeased, should speak thus:
‘I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training.’”
‘Only these ascetic women are true ascetic women, the daughters of the Sakyans;
there are other ascetic women who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training—in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
That bhikkhunī should be addressed by the bhikkhunīs thus:

“‘Noble lady, being angry and displeased, you spoke thus: “I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training. What indeed are these recluses who are daughters of the Sakyans?
There are other recluses who are modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life.”’”
‘I will practice, noble lady; the Dhamma is well-proclaimed. Practice the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.

If that bhikkhunī, being thus addressed by the bhikkhunīs, should still persist in her position, that bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhunīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that [position].
If, being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is good.
If she does not relinquish it, this nun too has committed an offense that is to be confessed after the third [admonition], an *saṅghādisesa* offense involving expulsion.
“Whoever” means whichever such person... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Angry and displeased" means:
Displeased, with hearts struck down and become callous, they might speak thus:
"I renounce the Buddha... [and so on] ...I renounce the training. What indeed are these nuns, who are nuns?"
“Daughters of the Sakyan, there are indeed nuns who are virtuous, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training;
in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
She is a bhikkhunī.
Regarding that nun who speaks thus:
"By the nuns" means by other nuns. Those who see her or hear her should say to her:
“Noble lady, being angry and displeased, you spoke thus:
‘I renounce the Buddha... [as before] ...I renounce the training.
What indeed are these ascetics, these daughters of the Sakyans?’”
‘There are indeed other female ascetics who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
‘Be joyful, noble lady! The Dhamma is well-proclaimed;
lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.’”
A second time she should be told;
a third time she should be told.
If she relinquishes it, that is good.
If she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having heard [the charge], if they do not speak, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
That nun should be dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha and addressed thus:
“Noble lady, being angry and displeased, you spoke thus:
‘I renounce the Buddha... [and so on] ...I renounce the training.
What have these ascetics to do with me, these ascetics who are daughters of the Sakyans?’”
‘There are other female ascetics who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
‘Delight, noble lady! The Dhamma is well-expounded;
lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.’”
It should be said a second time.
It should be said a third time.
If she relinquishes it, that is good.
If she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
That bhikkhunī is to be formally admonished.
And thus, monks, is she to be formally admonished:
The Saṅgha should be informed by a competent and capable bhikkhunī:
“Venerable ladies, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This bhikkhunī named so-and-so, being angry and displeased, speaks thus:”
“I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training.
What indeed are these ascetics, these daughters of the Sakyans?
There are other ascetics who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training; in their presence I shall lead the holy life.”
She does not relinquish that matter.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha formally admonish the bhikkhunī so-and-so for the sake of relinquishing that matter.
This is the motion.
"Let the Saṅgha, noble ladies, hear me.
This bhikkhunī named so-and-so, being angry and displeased, speaks thus:
‘I renounce the Buddha... [and so on] ...I renounce the training.’"
“Let there be only those female ascetics who are daughters of the Sakyans;
let there be other female ascetics as well who are modest, conscientious, and desirous of training—in their presence I shall lead the holy life.
Yet she did not relinquish that course of action.
The Saṅgha exhorts the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
Whichever noble lady approves of the exhortation of the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter, let her be silent;
whichever does not approve, let her speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
A third time I speak this matter...
The Saṅgha has formally admonished the bhikkhunī named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
"It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the motion (*ñatti*);
there are offenses of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*) for the two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*).
At the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
For one who commits a *saṅghādisesa*, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the motion (*ñatti*); by two formal proclamations, the grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) are extinguished.
This too—
It is said with reference to the preceding [offenses].
"Up to the third time" means that one incurs [the offense] through being exhorted up to three times, not simultaneously with the transgression of the matter itself.
"Leading to expulsion" means one is expelled from the Saṅgha.
"Saṅghādisesa" [means...]
... [as before] ... for that reason also it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act, one perceives it as a legitimate legal act and does not desist, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act, one is doubtful and does not desist, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
If it is an illegal act, but one perceives it as a legal act and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If it is an illegal act, but one perceives it as a legal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegal act, but one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense for one who does not admonish [the monks].
For one who relinquishes it,
for one who is insane,
and for one who is a first-time offender.
The training rule on the seventh Saṅghādisesa is finished.
